accessibility.semantics.reason: Reviewed the fresh DOM heading outline and Chrome accessibility tree against the retained core-page structure. Meaningful activity/contact/service headings and native navigation regions exist, but the sampled pages lack a main landmark and expose multiple unnamed navigation regions without contextual labels; the contact/service outlines also jump from H1 to H3 sidebar sections. Partial credit records limited structural orientation. Missing main or skipped heading levels alone are not called automatic WCAG failures. Fresh resource exclusions remain recorded, and the same structural omissions are corroborated in the retained observations.

accessibility.language-aria.reason: The fresh sampled Arabic content agrees with the root ar declaration, and native/ARIA control names are exposed in the accessibility tree. However, several visible contact inputs carry aria-describedby references whose target elements do not exist in the captured DOM. Partial credit records these unresolved description references; correct labels are not treated as missing, and unmounted targets of closed menus/comboboxes are not the basis. This is a sampled ARIA-usage defect, not a complete WCAG or screen-reader conformance claim.

Reviewed the three fresh representative Arabic pages and their actual language declarations. The root ar declarations match the main content, but the visible contact-form wrapper overrides its Arabic labels, governorate options and instructions with lang=en-US. Partial credit records this specific incorrect language-of-parts override; no form was submitted and no complete screen-reader conformance is claimed.

Arabic root declarations match the principal sampled content, but six visible dropdown triggers on each core page are generic SPAN elements with no interactive role and tabindex=-1 while carrying aria-expanded and aria-haspopup. Manual inspection of the captured elements corroborates the aria-allowed-attr findings: the expanded state is attached to unsupported generic semantics. Partial credit records this ARIA implementation defect, not an inferred failure of every keyboard interaction or all assistive technology.
